passages.title: The Human Heart
paragraphs: Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel it? Thump, thump, thump. That is your heart. It never stops working. Not even for one second, your whole life. Your heart is about the size of your closed fist. Its job is to be a pump. It pushes blood all around your body. It uses long, thin tubes called blood vessels.

Inside your heart there are four rooms. We call them chambers. Blood comes in from your body. It is low on oxygen. The heart sends it to your lungs. There it picks up fresh oxygen. Then the blood comes back to the heart. The heart pushes it out again. It goes to every part of you. It goes to your brain, your fingers, and your toes. It carries fresh oxygen to keep every part of you working. Blood goes around this whole loop about once every minute. That is why oxygen is so vital. Without it, your body's parts cannot do their jobs. A doctor listening to your heartbeat is really listening to that pump. It works over and over, to keep you alive.

questions.q: How many chambers does the heart have?

passages.title: The Human Heart
paragraphs: Anyone can check how hard their heart is working. You only need two fingers and a watch.

Press your first two fingers gently on the inside of your wrist, just below your thumb. Or press them against the side of your neck. You will feel a steady beat. This is your pulse. Each beat is one push of your heart, sending blood out into your body.

A resting adult heart usually beats sixty to a hundred times a minute. A lower number, within reason, is often a sign of a fit heart. Regular exercise trains the heart muscle. A trained heart can pump more blood with each beat. So it does not need to beat as often to circulate the same amount of blood.
A higher number can mean stress, illness, too much caffeine, or simply climbing a flight of stairs. The number alone does not tell the whole story.
Doctors and nurses check pulse all the time. It is one of the fastest, cheapest ways to learn something important about a person's health, without any equipment beyond a watch.

Knowing your own normal resting pulse is useful. Check it while you are resting, not right after activity. This gives you a baseline. If your pulse ever feels clearly different from normal, especially if it feels uneven rather than just fast or slow, it is worth mentioning to a doctor. Do not just ignore it.
